criteria.dispatch_only_revoke: End every token inside dispatch: keep the existing materialize-then-abandon shape and add revocation to the same finally for handled and rejected paths alike, accepting that handled tokens die before owner drainage finishes.
criteria.server_only_revoke: Keep dispatch as abandon-only and revoke exactly once in the server outer finally after the per-request scope drains; direct dispatch callers without a server scope must revoke retained tokens themselves or accept that they stay live.
criteria.split_boundary: Divide the duty: dispatch abandons the unread body and additionally revokes on rejected-route paths where no handler ran, while the server outer boundary revokes handled tokens after owner drainage in a finally before returning the response; the revoke primitive is idempotent so the overlap is safe.

revocation_boundary.instructions: Where should request-capability revocation live so handled, failed, rejected, upgrade, and unread-body paths all end the token without breaking admitted child work?

criteria.silent_idempotent: revokeRequest deletes the token from every table and silently ignores unknown, forged, or already-revoked input so it is safe to call in finally paths and twice on one request.
criteria.throw_unknown: revokeRequest throws the resource-state failure for unknown or already-revoked input so caller mistakes surface loudly, and every finally call site must prove its argument is a live token.

revoke_failure_mode.instructions: What failure mode should the revokeRequest primitive use for unknown or already-revoked input?

state.lifetime_requirements: The mandated sequence is fixed: the handler settles and its response or upgrade decision is materialized, any unread live body is abandoned, the per-request owner scope drains admitted child work, and only then the outer request boundary revokes the token in a finally path before the native response returns. Retained header, body, snapshot, and upgrade operations must fail with the resource-state failure, and only after that lifetime ends: child work that touches the token during drainage must still succeed. Buffered requests are revoked exactly like lazy ones, and neither a failed handler nor a rejected route may leak a usable token.
state.mandate: Can is an AI-agent-authored language with zero external users and no compatibility obligation. This task ends the server request capability after body cleanup and owner drainage. The mandated order is fixed; you advise only the mechanism split between dispatch and the server boundary plus the revoke primitive failure mode, from the supplied evidence. You cannot inspect source or run code.
state.production_paths: The production path snapshots the native request into a frozen token, binds the upgrade server, runs serveSnapshot inside one per-request owner scope (action match or legacy dispatch into the handler), converts the handler value to a native response, abandons any unread live body, drains the scope, and returns the response with server leases released. Dispatch is also invoked directly by tests and harnesses without any server scope. A rejected route (unknown path or wrong method) runs no handler, so nothing in that scope can capture the token. A WebSocket upgrade claims the native request and server inside the handler, keeps the socket and server object on the session rather than the token, and returns a sentinel instead of an HTTP reply. Shutdown must preserve leases and close once; the dispatch boundary is handed to a later captured-routes task, so the change must stay small and explicit.
state.token_mechanism: Each request is a frozen empty object used as a key in four WeakMaps: an immutable head-plus-body snapshot, a body cell that is either buffered bytes or a live single-use wire stream, an optional upgrade-server binding, and an upgrade-claimed set. Abandoning a request only cancels an unread live body stream and leaves all four tables intact, so both buffered and lazy tokens stay recognized afterwards; a Bun 1.4.2 probe executing snapshot plus abandon plus re-read demonstrates exactly that. Every header, body, snapshot, and upgrade operation already consults these tables first and throws the resource-state failure for unknown keys, so deleting a token from all four tables revokes the whole capability at once.
